lead: A shared link needs one rule at every instant: who may transmit now? A medium access protocol is that rule. Stations compete, take turns, or own a slice in advance. The competing family — ALOHA, CSMA, CSMA/CD and CSMA/CA — is what most syllabi mean by multiple access protocols. CSMA/CD shaped shared-cable Ethernet; CSMA/CA runs on Wi-Fi. Switched full-duplex Ethernet no longer needs CSMA/CD. This chapter gives the throughput formulas, collision rules and timings.
prereq: You need 3.1 for the frame, and propagation delay and bit rate from Unit 2.

blocks.text: Two stations that start together send overlapping signals. The receiver hears noise and both frames are lost. A medium access protocol decides who talks, and how to recover from a clash.

items: Random access: stations compete. Anyone may send when the channel looks free; the protocol says how to back off after a clash. ALOHA, CSMA, CSMA/CD and CSMA/CA are here.
Controlled access: stations take turns. Polling has a master ask each station in turn; token passing circulates a token frame and only its holder may send.
Channelisation: the channel is split in advance: one frequency per station (FDMA), one time slot (TDMA), or one code (CDMA). See Unit 2.

blocks.text: Pure ALOHA is the simplest random rule. A station with a frame sends at once, without sensing, then waits for an acknowledgement. If none arrives it waits a random time and retries.
The weakness is the vulnerable time. Let a frame last T seconds. Another frame ruins ours if it starts from T before our first bit to T after it, a window of 2T.

blocks.where: S is throughput as a fraction of channel capacity, G is offered load in frames per frame time, and e = 2.718. S peaks at G = 0.5 with S = 0.184, so about 82 percent is wasted.

blocks.text: Slotted ALOHA cuts the window in half. Time is divided into slots of one frame time T, and a frame may start only at a slot boundary. Frames collide only if they begin in the same slot, so the window is T; G is per slot.

blocks.where: S and G are as before. The maximum is 0.368 at G = 1, twice pure ALOHA.

blocks.text: CSMA adds one habit: listen before you talk. A station senses the channel; if it hears a carrier it waits, if idle it transmits. This removes most collisions, not all.

The leftover danger is propagation delay. Suppose A starts at time 0. Its signal needs τ seconds to reach B. If B senses at τ − ε the channel is still silent, B starts too, and frames overlap. The danger window shrinks from a frame time to one propagation delay τ.

items: 1-persistent: sense; if busy keep sensing; the moment it is idle send with probability 1. Greedy, so collisions are likely when many wait.
Non-persistent: if busy, wait a random time and sense again. Fewer collisions, longer delays.
p-persistent: on an idle slotted channel, send with probability p and defer with probability 1 − p. A compromise.

blocks.text: CSMA/CD adds collision detection for a half-duplex cable. While sending, the station listens and compares what it hears with what it sends. When they differ, a collision is in progress. It sends a short jam signal so others notice too, then stops and backs off.

items: Sense the channel. If busy, wait and sense again.
If idle, start transmitting and keep monitoring the cable.
If the received signal differs from the transmitted signal, a collision has occurred.
Send a short jam signal, then stop transmitting.
Wait k slot times, then retry from step 1.

blocks.text: slot time = 2τ,   minimum frame = 2τ × bit rate
blocks.where: τ is one-way propagation delay in seconds, so 2τ is the round trip. The minimum frame guarantees the sender is still transmitting when the collision signal returns; a shorter frame is padded, otherwise the sender would finish early and never learn of the collision.

blocks.text: Backoff is binary exponential. After the i-th collision the station picks k uniformly from {0, 1, …, 2i − 1} and waits k slot times. Early collisions give short waits; repeated collisions spread stations apart. The exponent is capped, and after too many failures the frame is dropped and reported.

CSMA/CA avoids collisions instead of detecting them. A radio cannot listen while it transmits and has hidden terminals. A station waits until the channel is idle, waits an interframe gap, then runs a random backoff counter that decreases only while the channel is silent. The receiver acknowledges every frame, so a lost frame is detected by a missing ACK. Optional RTS/CTS frames reserve the medium. Details are in 3.9.

figure.caption: Throughput S against offered load G for the two ALOHA rules. The dots mark the worked example's peaks: 0.184 at G = 0.5 for pure ALOHA, and 0.368 at G = 1 for slotted ALOHA, exactly double.

spec.aria: Two curves of throughput S against offered load G: pure ALOHA peaks at 0.184 when G is 0.5, and slotted ALOHA peaks at 0.368 when G is 1, both peaks marked with dots.

examples.question: Frames of 1000 bits share one channel. (a) At G = 0.5 frame per frame time, find pure ALOHA throughput as a fraction of the channel. (b) Find slotted ALOHA throughput at its best point G = 1. (c) A CSMA/CD LAN runs at 10 Mbps with round-trip time 2τ = 51.2 μs. Find the slot time in bits and the minimum frame length in bytes.
steps: Pure ALOHA: S = G × e<sup>−2G</sup> with G = 0.5, so 2G = 1 and e<sup>−1</sup> = 0.3679.
S = 0.5 × 0.3679 = 0.1839, that is 18.4 percent of the channel.
Slotted ALOHA: S = G × e<sup>−G</sup> with G = 1, so e<sup>−1</sup> = 0.3679.
S = 1 × 0.3679 = 0.3679, that is 36.8 percent, exactly twice the pure ALOHA figure.
Slot time in bits = 2τ × bit rate = 51.2 × 10<sup>−6</sup> s × 10 000 000 bit/s = 512 bits.
Minimum frame = 512 bits ÷ 8 bit/byte = 64 bytes. Any shorter frame is padded to 64 bytes.
examples.answer: Pure ALOHA gives 18.4 percent, slotted ALOHA gives 36.8 percent, and the LAN needs 512 bits, that is a minimum frame of 64 bytes.
examples.check:
from math import exp
G1 = 0.5
print(round(G1 * exp(-2 * G1), 4))
G2 = 1.0
print(round(G2 * exp(-G2), 4))
round_trip = 51.2e-6
rate = 10e6
bits = round_trip * rate
print(round(bits, 4))
print(round(bits / 8, 4))

examples.question: A station on an Ethernet LAN has just suffered its third collision. Over how many slot times may it wait, and what is the largest wait if one slot time is 51.2 μs?
steps: For the i-th collision the set of slots is {0, 1, …, 2<sup>i</sup> − 1}.
Here i = 3, so 2<sup>3</sup> = 8 and k is uniform in {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7}.
The longest wait is k = 7 slots.
examples.answer: It waits k slot times with k uniform in {0, …, 7}, and the longest wait is 358.4 μs.
examples.check:
i = 3
slots = 2 ** i
print(slots)
print(slots - 1)
slot_time_us = 51.2
print(round((slots - 1) * slot_time_us, 4))

traps: Pure ALOHA uses e<sup>−2G</sup> and slotted ALOHA uses e<sup>−G</sup>. Swapping the exponents is the commonest slip in the chapter.
CSMA/CA has no collision detection and no jam signal. A radio cannot hear a collision while its transmitter is on, so 802.11 avoids clashes and ACKs every frame instead.
In the minimum-frame calculation, use round trip 2τ, not τ, and divide bits by 8 for bytes. At 10 Mbps and 2τ = 51.2 μs the answer is 512 bits = 64 bytes.

The backoff set after the i-th collision has 2<sup>i</sup> slots numbered 0 to 2<sup>i</sup> − 1, so the range is not 2 × i and not 1 to 2<sup>i</sup>. The count doubles per collision but stays capped.
G is offered load in frames per frame time, not a success probability. At G = 1 a slotted ALOHA channel carries only 0.368 frames per frame time; the rest collide.

quiz.q: What is the vulnerable time of pure ALOHA, and why?
quiz.a: 2T, twice the frame time T. A frame collides with any other frame that starts within T before or T after its own start.

quiz.q: Name the three families of medium access protocols with one example each.
quiz.a: Random access (ALOHA, CSMA), controlled access (polling, token passing) and channelisation (FDMA, TDMA, CDMA).

quiz.q: CSMA listens before transmitting, yet collisions still happen. Why?
quiz.a: Propagation delay. A station far away senses the channel before the first station's signal arrives, finds it idle, and transmits. The danger window is one propagation delay τ, not a full frame time.

1-persistent sends with probability 1 the instant the channel frees, so waiting stations collide often. Non-persistent waits a random time after finding the channel busy, which lowers collisions but raises delay.

quiz.q: A slotted ALOHA channel carries an offered load of G = 2 frames per frame time. Find its throughput.
quiz.a: S = G e<sup>−G</sup> = 2 × e<sup>−2</sup> = 2 × 0.1353 = 0.2707, about 27.1 percent of the channel. It is past the peak of 0.368 at G = 1.

quiz.q: A CSMA/CD LAN runs at 100 Mbps with 2τ = 5.12 μs. Find the slot time in bits and the minimum frame in bytes.
quiz.a: Slot time = 5.12 × 10<sup>−6</sup> × 100 000 000 = 512 bits. Minimum frame = 512 ÷ 8 = 64 bytes.

quiz.q: Why does IEEE 802.11 use CSMA/CA instead of CSMA/CD?
quiz.a: A radio cannot transmit and listen at the same time, so collisions cannot be detected; the hidden terminal problem makes sensing unreliable. 802.11 therefore avoids collisions with random backoff and confirms delivery with an ACK per frame.

beyond: Not for the exam. Wi-Fi 6 and later mix both families: the access point schedules uplink traffic in OFDMA resource units, which is channelisation, while random backoff handles unplanned traffic. Full-duplex switched Ethernet has no shared cable, so CSMA/CD is mostly textbook material. Research continues on collision resolution and full-duplex wireless, where a node cancels its own signal to listen while transmitting.
